feature.title: The Sunday five finance ministers moved the dollar: the Plaza Accord, 1985
body: With a trade summit on this week's calendar, here is the deal every currency desk still talks about. By early 1985 the dollar had climbed about 50% against the other major currencies in five years. Paul Volcker's high interest rates pulled money into the US, American exporters were being priced out of world markets, and Congress was drafting tariff bills aimed at Japan.

On Sunday, September 22, 1985, the finance ministers and central bankers of the US, Japan, West Germany, France and the UK met at the Plaza Hotel in New York. Treasury Secretary James Baker got what he wanted: a joint statement that the other currencies should rise against the dollar, backed by coordinated selling of dollars by all five central banks.

It worked faster than anyone planned. The yen went from about 240 per dollar to roughly 150 within about a year and a half. By February 1987 the same countries met at the Louvre in Paris to try to stop the slide.

The lesson desks draw is that intervention works when it is coordinated and when it pushes in the direction policy is already heading; US rates were falling by then. The warning is what came next: Japan cut rates to cushion the strong yen, an asset bubble followed, and it burst in 1990. Chinese officials still cite the Plaza Accord as the reason not to agree to a fast currency revaluation under pressure.

stories.headline: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns and CFO Colette Kress is named interim CEO; shares fall sharply
stories.dek: Nvidia's release and 8-K confirm the move, effective immediately; the board has opened a search, earnings proceed as scheduled, and Congress wants Huang to testify.
stories.updateNote: Added Thursday's close and Friday's volatile trading.
tldr: Nvidia's release and 8-K say **Jensen Huang resigned** as CEO on Nov. 12, effective immediately; **CFO Colette Kress** is interim CEO; **Harvey Jones** is board chair; a CEO search has begun.

The company **gave no reason**; Fortune and CNN tie the exit to personal conduct and a reported relationship with a woman US intelligence officials deemed a Chinese asset, which Nvidia has disputed in earlier statements.
Shares fell more than 13% at one point Thursday and closed down about 4.3% by one report; Friday was volatile and the Nasdaq fell 0.9%. Nvidia reports earnings next Tuesday.
whatHappened: Nvidia filed an [[8-K]] announcing that CEO Jensen Huang has resigned. CFO Colette Kress will serve as [[interim CEO]] and remain CFO until a permanent successor is named, board chair Harvey Jones said, and the board has begun a search that will consider internal and external candidates. The company did not give a reason for the departure. Fortune and CNN report that it followed mounting scandal tied to personal conduct and to a reported relationship with a woman that US intelligence officials deemed a Chinese asset; those details come from press reporting, not the filing, and Nvidia had previously disputed related reports.

Markets: Nvidia shares fell more than 13% at one point in early trading on Thursday before paring some of the loss, according to one report; Reports put Nvidia's Thursday close down about 4.3% after the early drop of more than 13%, and Friday's trading was volatile, swinging between gains and losses; the Nasdaq fell 0.91% Friday as Nvidia sold off, per CNBC. The Motley Fool described rival chipmakers surging, the Nasdaq Composite closed down about 0.4% and the S&P 500 about 0.35%, with Nvidia a heavy weight on both. The company is due to report earnings next Tuesday with no permanent CEO named.

**Follow-up:** Nvidia said its scheduled earnings report will proceed as planned. PBS reports that the House Foreign Affairs Committee chair, Brian Mast, said Huang is expected to testify before Thanksgiving and could be subpoenaed if needed; PBS also notes that Nvidia had earlier said Huang would stay on while the company investigated.
background: Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and led it from a graphics-chip maker to the center of the AI build-out, which made him unusually tied to the company's story. Last week the stock had already fallen about 5% on each of Monday and Tuesday on a New York Times report about a Megaspeed executive close to Huang, and on Dow Jones reports of an investigation. This resignation turns that headline risk into a leadership transition.

The risk investors price here is [[key-person risk|key-person risk]]: when one executive embodies a company's strategy and credibility, his exit raises questions about customers, partners and execution, even if the business is strong.
whyItMatters: Nvidia is one of the largest weights in the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq-100, so its moves swing the indexes. Tuesday's earnings now double as a test of whether customers keep ordering with an interim CEO, and of whether the AI trade can hold without its figurehead. Beneficiaries in the short term may be rival chip suppliers; AI spenders watch for supply or guidance changes.

grandLine.title: After Whitebeard fell
grandLine.body: When Whitebeard died at Marineford, a dominant power vanished and the whole New World repositioned at once, with volatility spiking. A founder-CEO leaving the company at the center of the AI trade is a smaller version: the business doesn't disappear, but everyone reprices who holds the power and what the next leader will do.

views.thesis: A strong franchise outlasts a CEO change.
views.argument: Demand for Nvidia's chips is real, Kress is a long-time CFO and known quantity, and the board has an orderly interim structure, so the drop overshoots.

views.thesis: The exit removes the company's central figure at a fragile moment.
views.argument: The AI trade was already shaky, the scandal involved alleged China links, and with no permanent CEO, customers and investors face more uncertainty into earnings.

interview.question: Nvidia's CEO resigned. How do you trade it?
interview.answer: I'd treat it as event volatility. [[Key-person risk]] justifies a discount, but the fundamentals and Tuesday's earnings matter more. I'd avoid a directional bet before the print and think about options or a pair versus a rival. What changes my mind is guidance: if demand commentary holds, the drop looks overdone; if customers pause orders, it's worse.

followUp.question: Why does an interim CEO matter?
followUp.answer: It signals continuity but also uncertainty: strategy decisions and big customer relationships can stall until a permanent leader is named.

trade.expression: Buy an NVDA straddle or strangle expiring after Tuesday's report, small size
trade.rationale: The CEO exit plus earnings creates a large, two-sided event. If the move exceeds what options price, the straddle pays. Interview framing, not advice.
risks: Implied volatility is already elevated, so it may overprice the move.
A muted reaction crushes option value.
A gap on the weekend or before earnings can hurt a short-dated position.

A temporary chief executive who leads while the board searches for a permanent one.

stories.headline: October producer prices rise 0.3%, cooler than the 0.4% expected, with core in line at 0.3%
stories.dek: The annual PPI rate is 6.5%, the highest since November 2022, but the monthly miss helped stocks early Friday; a December hike is still near-certain.
stories.updateNote: Replaced the preview with the October PPI result.
tldr: October PPI rose **0.3%** m/m vs. **0.4%** expected; core PPI rose **0.3%**, in line.
The annual PPI rate was **6.5%**, the highest since November 2022, per reports.
Stocks popped on the print but the Nasdaq ended down on Nvidia; a 25bp December hike is near-certain, with 50bp the debate.
whatHappened: The Bureau of Labor Statistics said the Producer Price Index rose 0.3% in October from September, below the 0.4% economists expected. [[Core PPI|core PPI]], which excludes food and energy, also rose 0.3%, in line with forecasts. The annual rate was reported at 6.5%, the highest since November 2022. Equity futures rose after the release and the major averages initially popped, though the Nasdaq finished lower on Nvidia. The data follows Tuesday's hot CPI (+0.4%, core +0.3%) and September's 1.3% PPI jump, so the cooler monthly number takes a little pressure off but doesn't change the hike debate.
background: PPI often leads consumer prices because producers pass costs on with a lag. Energy-heavy components can swing the headline, so economists watch core PPI (excluding food and energy) for the underlying trend.
whyItMatters: The December meeting is the next decision point, and the debate is 25bp versus 50bp. Data between now and then, starting with PPI, moves the [[2-year yield]] most because it tracks the expected policy path.

grandLine.title: Nami reads the sky
grandLine.body: Nami reads small signs in the air before committing to a heading. PPI is one of those signs: it shows what's building in the pipeline before it hits consumer prices, and traders read it for the weather the Fed will face next.

views.thesis: Hot producer prices mean more consumer inflation ahead.
views.argument: September PPI jumped, core ran well above forecast, and producers are passing costs on, which supports a bigger hike.

views.thesis: Energy's drop should ease PPI soon.
views.argument: Brent has fallen sharply from its peak, so energy components should cool, taking some heat out of the pipeline.

interview.question: What does PPI add after a hot CPI?
interview.answer: It tells you whether cost pressure is still building upstream. A hot core PPI reinforces the hike case and pushes the 2-year up; a soft one suggests CPI strength may be peaking. I'd compare core to consensus and look at trade and transport margins. What changes my mind is a big downside miss.

followUp.question: Why does core matter more?
followUp.answer: Food and energy swing a lot month to month, so core is a cleaner read on underlying pressure.

keyTerms.definition: The yield on the 2-year Treasury, which tracks the expected path of the Fed's policy rate.
Producer prices excluding food and energy; a cleaner read on underlying upstream inflation.

stories.headline: Wall Street ends a volatile week higher as Nvidia drags the Nasdaq down 0.9% on Friday
stories.dek: The S&P 500 rose about 2.5% on the week and the Nasdaq about 2.3%, its best week since August, despite a hot CPI, a 5% 10-year yield and Nvidia's CEO exit.
tldr: Friday close: **Dow +50.46 (+0.1%) to 52,347.55**, **S&P 500 -0.4% to 7,561.67**, **Nasdaq -0.91% to 25,136.27** (the Nasdaq's best week since August).
Week: **S&P 500 +2.5%**, **Nasdaq +2.3%**, **Dow +2.1%**; sources differ slightly on the Friday levels.
October PPI came in cooler than expected: **+0.3%** vs. 0.4% forecast, with core +0.3% in line.
whatHappened: Stocks ended a whipsaw week with gains. On Friday the Dow edged up 50.46 points, or about 0.1%, to 52,347.55, while the S&P 500 fell about 0.4% to 7,561.67 and the Nasdaq Composite fell 0.91% to 25,136.27 as Nvidia's leadership turmoil kept weighing on tech, per CNBC and TheStreet; another recap had slightly different levels. Even so, the S&P 500 gained about 2.5% for the week, the Nasdaq about 2.3% (its best week since August) and the Dow about 2.1%. Money moved out of tech in a [[rotation]] and into other sectors, which helped the Dow, and [[breadth]] improved. The week included Monday's 1,104-point Dow rally on falling oil, Tuesday's hot CPI, Thursday's bond-market catch-up to a 5.1% 10-year, and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's resignation.
background: Last week's Nasdaq correction set a low base: the S&P 500 fell 2.7% the week before, its worst since June, so this week's gain is mostly a retrace. Oil's drop and a cooler PPI helped, while yields near 5% and the Nvidia story capped the rebound.
whyItMatters: The index is back near its highs, but leadership has shifted from tech to the rest of the market. That rotation is fragile if the 10-year keeps rising or if Nvidia's Tuesday earnings, the first without Huang, disappoint.

grandLine.title: The Straw Hats' navigator
grandLine.body: Nami doesn't steer by yesterday's weather; she reads the sky and adjusts. After a week that swung between storm and calm, the market's next heading hinges on two readings: Nvidia's report and the Fed minutes.

views.thesis: Money moving out of tech into the rest of the market broadens the rally.
views.argument: The Dow gained, small caps and cyclicals participated earlier in the week, and falling oil helps most sectors.

views.thesis: The AI leader's turmoil is the real risk.
views.argument: With Nvidia, the Nasdaq's heaviest weight, in disarray and 10-year yields near 5%, the rebound can reverse quickly.

interview.question: The S&P rose 2.5% on a week with hot CPI and a CEO resignation. How do you read it?
interview.answer: As a rebound from an oversold base helped by lower oil and a cooler PPI, not a clean all-clear. Breadth improved but tech is the swing factor and yields are near 5%. I'd watch Nvidia's Tuesday report and the FOMC minutes next Wednesday. What changes my mind is a break above 5.2% on the 10-year.

followUp.question: Why does PPI matter after CPI?
followUp.answer: It shows pipeline pressure; a cooler PPI eases fears that producer costs will keep pushing consumer prices up.

stories.headline: Trump and Xi are expected to meet at APEC in Shenzhen this week, with the trade truce already extended
stories.dek: The two sides pushed the truce's expiry into January before the summit, so the meeting is about tone; big announcements are expected to wait.
tldr: Trump and Xi are expected to meet on the sidelines of the APEC summit in Shenzhen this week, their third meeting this year, per the South China Morning Post.
The US-China trade truce, due to lapse on November 10, was extended by two months to January 10, 2027, the paper reports.
Negotiators are still working on concrete deals, and major announcements are expected to wait for the G20, so the bar for a positive surprise is low.
whatHappened: China hosts this year's Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, and the South China Morning Post reports that Presidents Donald Trump and Xi Jinping are expected to meet there, for the third time this year. A briefing from the advisory firm BowerGroupAsia puts the leaders' meeting on November 18 and 19. Vladimir Putin is also expected to attend.

The most market-sensitive item was settled in advance. The [[trade truce]] the two leaders struck in Busan last year was due to expire on November 10. After talks in September, both governments extended it by two months, to January 10, 2027, with China announcing its extension days after Washington did, the paper reports.

What is not settled is substance. Negotiators have been racing to line up concrete trade and investment deals, and the same reporting says the major [[deliverables]] are expected to wait for the G20. I could not confirm from a second outlet that Trump's attendance is final.
background: A truce here means each side suspends the tariffs and export restrictions it had threatened, for a fixed period. It is a pause, with an expiry date, and each extension resets the clock. That is why markets care about the date more than the photo: a lapse would bring back higher tariffs on Chinese goods and China's limits on exports such as rare earths, which feed into chip and auto supply chains.
APEC itself is a 21-economy forum that produces statements, not treaties. Its value to markets is the meetings on the sidelines.
whyItMatters: With the truce extended, the downside scenario (a lapse this month) is off the table, so the summit carries more [[headline risk]] than fundamental risk. The assets that move on US-China tone are semiconductors, industrial exporters, soybeans and the yuan. It also lands in the same week as Nvidia's earnings, and Nvidia's China data-center revenue is close to zero under export controls, so any hint on chip rules matters for that stock too.

grandLine.title: A Reverie where the big vote waits
grandLine.body: At the Reverie, the world's kings gather at Mary Geoise, and once in a long while they vote to abolish an entire system, as they did with the Seven Warlords. Most of the time it is speeches. Shenzhen looks like the speeches kind: the truce was renewed before anyone arrived, and the decisions that would change the rules are expected at a later table.

views.thesis: The extension was the news; the meeting just confirms a stable relationship.
views.argument: Both governments chose to extend before the summit, and this is the third leader meeting this year. That pattern says neither side wants a blow-up, so tariff risk stays priced out into January.

views.thesis: Nothing new is on offer, so the risks are one-sided.
views.argument: If the deliverables wait for the G20, a good meeting changes little, while a stumble on chips, rare earths or Taiwan would hit semis and exporters. The extension is only two months, so the cliff comes back in January.

interview.question: Trump and Xi meet this week. Does that change how you'd position?
interview.answer: Not much. The market-moving piece, the truce extension to January, already happened, so the meeting is headline risk more than a catalyst. I'd expect a constructive tone and few deliverables. I wouldn't chase China-sensitive names into it, because the upside is small and a bad headline on chips or rare earths cuts the other way. What would change my mind is a concrete tariff rollback or a longer truce, which would be a real change in the path.

followUp.question: Which assets are most sensitive to US-China headlines?
followUp.answer: Semiconductors and industrial exporters in equities, soybeans in commodities, and the offshore yuan in FX. Rare-earth supply is the channel that hits autos and chips.

keyTerms.definition: A time-limited agreement to suspend threatened tariffs and export restrictions. It has an expiry date and has to be extended or replaced.
keyTerms.example: The Busan truce was due to lapse on November 10 and now runs to January 10, 2027.

keyTerms.definition: The concrete, announceable outcomes of a summit, such as a purchase commitment or a tariff cut, as opposed to statements of intent.
The risk that a news headline moves a price sharply even when the underlying fundamentals have not changed.

stories.headline: Nvidia reports Tuesday with the Street near $109 billion in revenue, on Colette Kress's first call as interim CEO
stories.dek: The company's own guide is about $108 billion, give or take 2%. The question is whether the outlook holds without Jensen Huang.
tldr: Nvidia reports fiscal third-quarter results Tuesday at about 4:20 PM ET, with the call at 5:00 PM ET, per its SEC filing.
Guidance is about $108 billion of revenue, plus or minus 2%; analysts expect about $109 billion and adjusted EPS near $2.47.
It is the first report since Huang resigned and CFO Colette Kress became interim CEO.
whatHappened: Nvidia kept its earnings date after last week's leadership change: results come Tuesday after the close, about 1:20 PM Pacific, with the call at 2:00 PM Pacific, according to the company's filing. Previews put consensus at roughly $109 billion of revenue and about $2.47 to $2.48 of adjusted earnings per share, against company guidance of about $108 billion, plus or minus 2%. Kress, who set that guidance as CFO, now has to defend it as interim CEO. Analysts are watching gross margin, which she said in August would bottom in the fourth quarter, supply commitments, and China, where data-center revenue is near zero.
whyItMatters: Nvidia is the largest weight in the Nasdaq and the reference point for AI spending, so its outlook sets the tone for tech into year-end. After Friday's selloff in the stock, the bar is the forward guide and how convincingly a new voice delivers it, more than the quarter itself.

stories.headline: COP31 enters its final week in Antalya with climate finance the main focus and no US delegation
stories.dek: About 190 countries are at the UN climate summit in Türkiye, which runs through Friday. Washington sent no officials for a second year.
tldr: The UN climate summit runs November 9–20 in Antalya, Türkiye, with representatives of about 190 countries.
The US sent no officials for the second straight year, after withdrawing from the Paris Agreement earlier in 2026.
whatHappened: COP31 opened in Antalya on November 9 and is scheduled to close on November 20. Türkiye's summit president, Murat Kurum, has said the aim is to turn earlier pledges into action, with financing the main focus. Leaders met in the first week; the second week is when negotiators try to settle a final text. The Trump administration did not send representatives.
whyItMatters: The outcome shapes how much public money flows to energy transition in developing countries, which matters for renewables, grid and nuclear suppliers. With the US absent, the weight of any deal falls on the EU, China and the host.
